title: Chapter 9: Collections and Data-Structure Choice
description: Choose collections from a workload rather than habit. The learner compares list, set, map, queue, deque, hash, tree, and linked-order contracts; analyzes complexity and memory locality; connects HashMap correctness to equality; distinguishes immutable snapshots from unmodifiable views; and documents every ordering and ownership promise exposed to callers.

lessons.title: Collection, List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque contracts
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Collection, List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque contracts

## Start from required operations
List preserves positional order and permits duplicates. Set models uniqueness. Map associates one value per key. Queue and Deque model work ordering. These interfaces do not all share null, mutability, concurrency, or iteration-order guarantees.

```java
java.util.List<String> visits = java.util.List.of("A", "B", "A");
java.util.Set<String> distinct = new java.util.HashSet<>(visits);
java.util.Map<String, Integer> counts = new java.util.HashMap<>();
for (String visit : visits) counts.merge(visit, 1, Integer::sum);
```
The list has three elements; the set has two; the map records A=2 and B=1. Hash-based iteration order is unspecified.

## Cost model
ArrayList indexed access is O(1), scanning a list is O(n), and hash lookup is expected O(1) under suitable hashing. Tree lookup is O(log n). Complexity describes growth, not exact duration; object allocation and locality still matter.

## Practice
Choose structures for ordered receipts, unique usernames, lookup by task ID, and breadth-first work. State duplicate and ordering policies. Test empty data and missing keys. Explain why changing List to Set can alter semantics even when it improves lookup speed.

exercises.title: Collection, List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque contracts: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Which abstraction associates one value with each unique key?
hints: Recall that Map is the abstraction with a one-to-one key-to-value association; List and Queue organize elements by position or processing order instead.

lessons.title: ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and memory locality
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and memory locality

## Array-backed versus linked storage
ArrayList stores references in a resizable array. Indexed access is fast, append is amortized constant-time, and inserting at the front shifts existing references. LinkedList uses separate linked nodes; walking to index i requires traversal and each node adds memory overhead. It is not automatically faster for insertions when locating the insertion point costs O(n).

## Stack and queue with Deque
```java
var work = new java.util.ArrayDeque<String>();
work.addLast("first");
work.addLast("second");
System.out.println(work.removeFirst()); // first
work.push("urgent");
System.out.println(work.pop()); // urgent
```
Deque can express FIFO or LIFO deliberately. pollFirst returns null for empty; removeFirst throws. ArrayDeque rejects null, so absence remains distinguishable. Java also ships an older `java.util.Stack` class for LIFO use, but it extends `Vector` and synchronizes every method, adding locking overhead most single-threaded code does not need; `ArrayDeque` is the preferred modern stack implementation instead.

## Practice
Implement undo using push/pop and BFS using addLast/removeFirst. Explain how mixing these directions changes traversal order. Compare indexed traversal of ArrayList and LinkedList; an index-based loop over LinkedList can become quadratic. Use an iterator when sequential traversal is intended. Do not claim performance from one tiny timing run; identify operations and data sizes first.

exercises.title: ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and memory locality: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why is repeated indexed traversal expensive for LinkedList?
choices: Each index lookup may traverse nodes
LinkedList stores its nodes contiguously, so indexing is just as fast as ArrayList
hints: Recall that LinkedList has no contiguous backing array; get(i) must walk node-to-node from an end, so an index-based loop over it can become quadratic.

lessons.title: HashMap and HashSet internals, equality, and collisions
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# HashMap and HashSet internals, equality, and collisions

## Hashing finds candidates, equality finds a key
HashMap computes a hash to locate a bucket, then checks equality among candidates. Collisions are legal. Equal keys must have equal hash codes, and keys must stay stable while stored.
```java
var counts = new java.util.HashMap<String, Integer>();
for (String word : java.util.List.of("red", "blue", "red")) {
    counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
}
System.out.println(counts.get("red")); // 2
System.out.println(counts.containsKey("green")); // false
```
get returning null can mean absence or a mapped null value. containsKey distinguishes these for maps allowing null. computeIfAbsent is useful for grouped containers, but callbacks should not perform surprising recursive modifications.

## Capacity and resizing
A load factor controls when storage expands. Pre-sizing a known large workload can reduce resizing, but allocating enormous maps speculatively wastes memory. HashMap is not thread-safe; concurrent updates need another design.

## Practice
Implement word frequencies with an explicit normalization policy. Test duplicate words, empty input, case differences, and a mutable-key counterexample. Explain why printing a HashMap cannot define a stable report order; sort entries or use an ordered implementation.

exercises.title: HashMap and HashSet internals, equality, and collisions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What resolves a hash collision between candidate keys?
choices: Assuming matching hashes imply identical keys
hints: Recall that hashing only narrows the search to one bucket of candidates; equality checking among those candidates is what confirms or rejects a true match.

lessons.title: TreeMap, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap, and ordering
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# TreeMap, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap, and ordering

## Two kinds of order
TreeMap and TreeSet keep comparator order with logarithmic core operations. LinkedHashMap and LinkedHashSet preserve insertion order. Access-order LinkedHashMap can support a simple least-recently-used policy but still needs a capacity rule and synchronization if shared.
```java
var deadlines = new java.util.TreeMap<Integer, String>();
deadlines.put(10, "review");
deadlines.put(3, "build");
System.out.println(deadlines.firstKey()); // 3
System.out.println(deadlines.ceilingKey(4)); // 10
```
Navigable maps support floor, ceiling, and bounded views. Views can be backed by the original map, so mutability and range restrictions matter. When every key or element is a constant of one enum type, `EnumSet` and `EnumMap` are specialized, more memory-efficient ordered alternatives to a general-purpose `HashSet<SomeEnum>` or `HashMap<SomeEnum, V>`: both are backed by a compact array indexed by the constant's ordinal rather than by hashing, and they iterate in the enum's natural declaration order.

## Comparator uniqueness
A TreeSet considers compare(a,b)==0 the same position. Sorting tasks by priority alone can collapse different tasks with equal priority. Add an ID tie-breaker when identity must remain distinct.

## Practice
Build an insertion-ordered audit report and a deadline-indexed task query. Explain why they need different structures. Test lower and upper range boundaries and whether the range view reflects later source changes. State when a sorted list is simpler than maintaining a tree continuously.

exercises.title: TreeMap, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap, and ordering: concept check
hints: Recall that LinkedHashMap augments hashing with an internal linked list that records insertion order, unlike plain HashMap whose iteration order is unspecified.

lessons.title: Unmodifiable views, immutable snapshots, and defensive copies
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Unmodifiable views, immutable snapshots, and defensive copies

## View versus snapshot
```java
var source = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("A"));
var view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
var snapshot = java.util.List.copyOf(source);
source.add("B");
System.out.println(view);     // [A, B]
System.out.println(snapshot); // [A]
```
The view blocks mutation through its API but reflects changes made through source. The snapshot captures the element references at copy time. Both remain shallow: a mutable element can change internally.

List.of and List.copyOf reject null elements. An unmodifiable list is not necessarily deeply immutable. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed by an array: set may work while add/remove do not.

## Practice
Design a repository's allTasks return contract. Should callers see a current live view or a stable snapshot? Should they mutate tasks themselves? Test changes to the original collection, returned collection, and one element separately. Explain why returning a mutable internal list lets a caller bypass repository validation even when the field itself is private.

exercises.title: Unmodifiable views, immutable snapshots, and defensive copies: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: After changing the source list, which result reflects it?
choices: An unmodifiable view backed by that list
Neither can ever reflect element changes
hints: Recall that Collections.unmodifiableList wraps the original list rather than copying it, so mutations made through the original reference are still visible through the view.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 9 assessment

Draw on this chapter's coverage of collection contracts, hashing, and ordering to work through the decision scenario and repair **Comparator ties**, a lab where a TreeSet's single-field comparator collapses two distinct records into one position. Write a prediction before running the debugger and preserve the intended distinctness when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

Implement `frequency`. Count how many strings equal target using case-sensitive content equality. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Array and its elements and target are non-null.

exercises.title: Comparator ties
exercises.instructionMarkdown: The `TreeSet` is ordered by a comparator that compares only `age`, so "Ada" and "Lin" — both 30 — are treated as the same set position and the second insert is silently dropped, leaving a size of `1` instead of `2`. Repair the comparator with a tie-breaker (for example, on name) so both distinct people are retained, keeping the demonstrated inserts, and explain why the tie-breaker fixes the count; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended operation requires source review.
hints: Preserve distinct names when ages tie by adding a comparator tie-breaker.
